note:
TIN PAN ALLEY — New York 1924. West 28th Street between Fifth and
Broadway, where the song-publishing trade kept its cubicles and its
upright pianos, and 1924 is the year the SONG the whole business was
built to sell reached its finished shape: Youmans and Caesar's "Tea
for Two" (No, No, Nanette) and Gershwin's "Fascinating Rhythm" (Lady,
Be Good), both published in New York that year, both a thirty-two bar
chorus in four eight-bar phrases.
FIVE ROWS ABOVE ASKED FOR THIS ONE. `crooner` sings its repertory,
`swing` and `jazz` improvise over its chord grids, `doowop` harmonises
its cadences on a street corner and `detroitsoul` was written in a building
organised as a publishing house on purpose.
THE AXES: this anchor is FORM and ALPHABET and almost nothing else,
which is right, because a Tin Pan Alley song was SHEET MUSIC — the
sound was whoever bought it. Alphabet is the circle of fifths taken
seriously (ii-V-I, a secondary dominant on the way, a chorus that
modulates by thirds); Material is a two-bar cell SEQUENCED, which is
literally how "Tea for Two" is built; Cast is two — a plugger and a
piano, which is what the room contained.

LINEAGE: `parlor` (New York 1892) is the same trade one technology
earlier — the piano in the front room the sheet was sold for — and
`ragtime` (Sedalia 1899) is where the syncopation in the melody
came from. The alley is the parlor song with a rag's rhythm and a
publisher's discipline over the form.
PAID 2026-08-29, the debts round: "operetta" is `operetta`
(London 1878) — the chorus craft the Alley's own writers
apprenticed under. "vaudeville" examined and declined the same
day: a stage FORMAT, not a music (the debts round's foot).

ii-V-I twice, with the third phrase leaning on the relative minor:
the alley's own harmony, and the reason a jazz musician can still
read a 1924 chorus at sight in 2026.

WHO SINGS: the crooner's own mouth, which is what this
repertory was sung with the moment a microphone existed.

WEIGHTS RESCALED 2026-09-03 (the catalogue round, shift 3). This row's 3 declared shares summed to 1.20, and a row cannot be more than all of itself — the sum is a claim about how much of THIS record its named ancestors explain, so above 1 it is not a claim at all. Every RATIO here is the row's own and none of them moved; the total did, back onto the catalogue's own 0.05 grid: parlor .60→.50, ragtime .40→.35, operetta .20→.15. The row now attributes 1.00 of itself and keeps nothing as its own invention. Rescaling to 1 rather than to something smaller is the conservative reading on purpose: it credits this row with the SMALLEST invention consistent with what it already said, so no residue is asserted that nobody argued for. GENRES.md §2, `parents`.

THE SWING IS THE LINE'S; THERE IS NO DRUMMER TO SWING (2026-09-05, the swing
census). This row renders NO drum event at all, so its declared swing can
only ever be the players'. MEASURED over the whole record, as written
against `swing` forced to 0: 0 of 0 hits and 2,327 of 17,653 line events
moved at seed 1 (12,342 of 27,452 at seed 2, 3,209 of 11,407 at seed 3). A
cubicle on West 28th Street held a plugger and an upright piano and nothing
else; the row seats what the business had. The 0.15 is the song's — a
thirty-two bar chorus sung and played with a lift. Kept as declared.
label: New York 1924
cannot: AABA — the thirty-two-bar chorus with a bridge in the third eight is what this music INVENTED, and section order is a song fact decided by the composer, not a field an anchor can declare; `bars: 8` says how long a phrase is and nothing says which phrase comes back
the modulation up a semitone for the last chorus, which is the plugger's own trick and needs a key change inside one record
words: the chorus, a two-bar cell sequenced
